name: Mískito
confidence_why: Salamanca's 1988 MIT grammar and his 2008 overview, independently backed by the CIDCA grammar Miskitu Bila Aisanka (1985), put main stress on the first syllable with only a few listed exceptions (aisabé, umpira, sakuna); the only dissent is Morales Quant, Padilla Brown and Zapata Webb's 2007 orthography study, which claims a second stress class on the second syllable but rests largely on those same exception words, and Constenla's 1987 passing opinion that Miskito is tonal, which Salamanca 2008 flatly denies.
catalog_quote: Stress is on the initial syllable:'El accento prosódico en miskito recae prácticamente siepre en la primera sílaba de la palabra' (Miskitu bila asainka:25).All exceptions are due to morphological structuring.

new_statements.quote: 2. Stress. The stress in Miskitu is one of the few characteristics that is across all dialects and does not change. a) ACCENT. The stress is always on the first syllable of the words including enunciation on the first vowel. Ex: KLAKaia, ALkras, Aras. There are few exceptions to this rule, but for the sake of this grammar and the different dialects, it is unnecessary to describe. [...] b) TONE. Miskitu relies heavily on tone to express meaning. For example, as in English, the end of the sentence for a question will rise in tone. [...] If there is a situation where there is an emphasis in conversation, often the pitch will rise on the first syllable to truly enunciate and proclaim the point.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (src StressTyp2) codes Mískito as fixed initial stress (initial stress); Herlihy states stress is always on the first syllable across all dialects. Adds only the remark that a few undescribed exceptions exist and that emphatic intonation raises pitch on the (stressed) first syllable. Access note: the listed open_url (KU ScholarWorks root) and the item handle 1808/25656 could not be reached by automated download even with a browser User-Agent, and web.archive.org is unreachable; the same open KU deposit (oai:kuscholarworks.ku.edu:1808/25656) was obtained through the CORE open-access aggregator athttps://core.ac.uk/download/213426052.pdf(112 pp., text, no scanned needed).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable of every word, uniformly across Miskitu dialects; the author notes that a few unspecified exceptions exist but does not describe them. 'Tone' in this pedagogical work refers to sentence intonation and emphatic pitch/lengthening (question rise, emphatic raised pitch on the first syllable), not lexical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: 'There are few exceptions to this rule, but for the sake of this grammar and the different dialects, it is unnecessary to describe.' No exceptions are listed.
new_statements.identity_note: Herlihy's textbook is based on Miskitu as taught in the KU study-abroad program on the Honduran/Nicaraguan Moskitia coast; she explicitly says the initial-stress rule holds 'across all dialects'. No particular dialect restriction affects the stress statement.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Salamanca 1988 quotations are verbatim in the PDF we hold; only the page locator needs correcting (p. 46 and pp. 46-47, not 45 / 45-46; p. 64 correct). (2) Deciding source: a 380-pp MIT PhD grammar (1988) by the principal Miskito specialist, Glottolog's best grammar; its stress remarks are incidental but unambiguous (main stress on the leftmost vowel; vowel length and [h] licensed only there), and the same author's 2008 typological overview (downloaded, Letras 43:104) states flatly 'no hay tonos y el acento está siempre en la primera sílaba'. No phonology article or instrumental study of Miskitu stress is listed in Glottolog or CrossRef. sources.quote: Community/orthographic study (109 Wangki and Tawira speakers, interviews) arguing against strict initial stress: p.34 'La ortografía acentual del idioma miskitu es regida por un sistema de acentuación bifonética en el que afectan a las dos primeras sílabas de la palabra'; p.35 'Los hablantes tawira como los wangki han demostrado que además de llevarla en la primera tonal existe otras palabras que acentúan en la segunda sílaba tónica' (examples mayá, winá vs wina, kupia, tiara; long vowels, diphthongs and closed first syllables keep stress initial). It also quotes the grammar tradition verbatim
